title: The case for character-led offices
summary: Why constrained Grade A supply and flight-to-quality are creating an opening for thoughtfully repositioned heritage stock.

body.text: Manchester's office market is telling two stories at once. Headline take-up is subdued against the ten-year average, yet the best space in the city is letting faster, at higher rents, than at any point in the last cycle. The gap between the two is where we invest.
Supply is the story

Grade A availability in the city core sits close to historic lows, and the development pipeline has thinned as build costs and finance costs pushed marginal schemes below viability. Occupiers seeking a genuinely better workplace — the buildings that pull people back to the office — are choosing from a short list.

That scarcity does not only reward glass towers. Occupiers consistently tell agents the same three things matter: location, quality of amenity, and a building with a point of view. A restored Georgian terrace with original fireplaces and three-metre ceilings answers the third in a way no speculative floorplate can.
What repositioning has to get right

items: Floorplates that work hard: cellular heritage buildings suit teams of eight to forty — precisely the professional-services occupiers most committed to in-person work.
Environmental performance: retrofit must reach an EPC trajectory lenders accept, which means fabric-first upgrades planned with the conservation officer, not against them.
Amenity without pastiche: showers, cycle stores and shared hospitality delivered in a language the building can carry.

body.text: Our own experience at 22 St John Street bears this out. Enquiry levels through fit-out have been dominated by law firms and advisory boutiques who name the building's character first and the rent second.
The investment view

Character-led offices remain a small share of city-centre stock, and planning friction keeps it that way. For patient capital, buying well-located heritage buildings below replacement cost and restoring them to institutional standard remains one of the clearest arbitrage opportunities in the regional market.

title: Greater Manchester living
summary: Five demand signals shaping rental resilience across the city region—from graduate retention to transport-led regeneration.

body.text: Residential demand across Greater Manchester continues to outrun supply, but the pattern of that demand is shifting. Understanding where renters and buyers actually want to live — and why — matters more to returns than any headline growth figure.
1. Graduate retention keeps compounding

Greater Manchester retains more of its graduates than any UK city region outside London, and the retained cohort is increasingly settling in the towns around the core rather than the city centre itself. Altrincham, Sale and Stockport capture households leaving city-centre rentals for more space without giving up the commute.
2. The Metrolink premium is real and measurable

Homes within a ten-minute walk of a Metrolink stop command a rental premium of roughly eight to twelve per cent over comparable stock further out, and let materially faster. Transport-led locations also show shallower voids through weaker markets — resilience that matters more than peak rent.
3. Stockport is the region's regeneration story

A decade of patient public investment — the interchange, Stockroom, the Mayoral Development Corporation — is now visibly crowding in private capital. Our Court House and Davenport schemes sit directly in this corridor, and the occupier interest they attract already reflects it.
4. Family housing is the structural shortage

The development industry has delivered city-centre apartments at scale, but three-bedroom homes in walkable town centres remain chronically undersupplied. Schemes that deliver them — like Barrington Road — are effectively pre-sold by the local market.
5. Quality is the differentiator, not price

Across every submarket we track, well-specified stock lets at a premium and holds tenants longer. The average tenancy length in our completed buildings runs well ahead of the regional average — the strongest single predictor of net income.
Taken together, these signals argue for exactly the strategy Satis pursues: characterful, well-connected buildings in the towns and corridors where Greater Manchester's growth is actually landing.

title: Finding value beyond the core
summary: A closer look at Altrincham and Stockport as connected, amenity-rich submarkets with long-term potential.

body.text: City-centre pricing has recovered to the point where prime yields leave little room for error. The more interesting risk-adjusted returns now sit in the connected town centres around the core — places with their own gravity, not dormitories.
Altrincham: the template

Altrincham's market-hall-led revival is the most studied town-centre turnaround in the country, and its lesson is often misread. The market hall did not create the demand; it revealed it. A dense, affluent catchment was already there, waiting for a reason to spend its time and money locally.

For residential investors the consequence is a town where values have re-rated but where the quality of stock has not caught up with the quality of place. Chester House and Barrington Road are both bets on closing that gap.
Stockport: earlier in the curve

Stockport today prices like a town the market has not yet revisited, while its fundamentals — eight minutes to Piccadilly, a genuinely historic core, and the most active regeneration programme in the region — read like Altrincham a decade ago. Entry pricing reflects the old story; the exit will price the new one.
What we look for

items: A rail or Metrolink connection under twenty minutes to central Manchester
An existing high street with independent operators, not just national convenience
Public investment already committed, not merely promised
Buildings with inherent character that new-build competitors cannot copy

body.text: None of this is a call against the city centre, where we remain active. It is a reminder that the region's growth is polycentric — and that the market still prices the centre first and the towns later. That lag is the opportunity.

title: How to read a development appraisal
summary: GDV, profit on cost, IRR and equity multiple — what each measure actually tells you, and the questions worth asking of any scheme.

body.text: Every development we share with investors arrives with an appraisal. The vocabulary is standard across the industry, but the assumptions behind the numbers are where schemes are really won or lost. This short guide sets out how we use each measure — and how we suggest you interrogate them.
Gross development value

GDV is the forecast end value of the completed scheme: units multiplied by expected pricing, or income capitalised at an exit yield. It is the biggest number on the page and the least certain. The question to ask is always the same — what comparable evidence supports the pricing, and how recent is it?
Profit on cost

Total forecast profit divided by total development cost. It measures the scheme's margin of safety: a development appraised at twenty per cent profit on cost can absorb meaningful cost inflation or price softening before investor capital is at risk. We do not bring schemes to investors below our internal threshold.
IRR and the equity multiple

The internal rate of return annualises your return, so it rewards speed; the equity multiple measures how much your money grows, so it rewards patience. A short deal can show a high IRR and a thin multiple. We publish both on every holding in this platform because either one alone can flatter a scheme.
Five questions we ask of every appraisal

items: What single assumption moves the outcome most, and what is the evidence for it?
How much contingency sits in the build cost, and who bears overruns beyond it?
What is the exit if the sales market pauses — can the scheme let and refinance instead?
When is investor capital drawn, and when does it realistically return?
What has to be believed about the location that is not already in the price?

body.text: If any figure in your holdings reporting is unclear, the investor relations team will happily walk through the underlying appraisal with you.

title: From consent to completion: managing programme risk
summary: How we structure procurement, contingency and reporting so that construction risk is carried by the people best placed to manage it.

body.text: Planning permission is the moment a scheme's value is created on paper; the two years that follow are where it is protected or eroded. Programme discipline — more than any market call — is what separates developments that deliver their appraisal from those that explain why they didn't.
Procurement before pricing

We tender the trades that carry the most cost risk — frame, envelope, MEP — before finalising the funding appraisal, so the numbers investors see reflect real market pricing rather than a quantity surveyor's hope. On heritage buildings we open up and survey before we commit: the most expensive surprises live behind plaster.
Contingency with rules

Every scheme carries a build contingency plus a separate programme reserve, and drawing either requires a documented cause, not a rounding exercise. Contingency that survives to completion returns to scheme profit — which is why our teams treat it as theirs to protect.
Reporting you can act on

items: Monthly cost reports reconcile committed, spent and forecast cost against the funding appraisal.
Programme is tracked against the contract baseline, with float shown honestly rather than absorbed silently.
Investor updates in this platform are drawn from the same reports the board sees — not a separate marketing narrative.

body.text: None of this removes construction risk; nothing does. The aim is narrower and more useful — that every risk is priced, owned by someone equipped to manage it, and visible to you before it becomes a variance.

title: Why we stay in Greater Manchester
summary: Depth of demand, a decade of transport investment and a planning environment we know street by street — the case for concentration.

body.text: Investors sometimes ask why Satis does not diversify into other regions. The honest answer is that concentration, done properly, is a risk-management strategy — not the absence of one.
Depth you can underwrite

Greater Manchester is the UK's largest economy outside London, with a population still growing ahead of the national rate. Demand this deep forgives timing errors that thinner markets punish: a scheme completing into a soft quarter here still lets; the same scheme in a shallow market sits empty.
Knowledge that compounds

Every planning committee, every conservation officer, every ground condition we have dealt with makes the next scheme cheaper to underwrite. We know which streets flood, which councils determine on time and what a facade retention really costs — knowledge that does not travel, and that a newcomer pays tuition to acquire.
A pipeline we can walk to

Our team can be on any of our sites within forty minutes. When a problem surfaces on a heritage refurbishment, the difference between hearing about it in a monthly report and standing in front of it that afternoon is measured in weeks of programme and real money.

We will follow the region's growth where it leads — as our work in Stockport shows. But the discipline holds: we invest where our information advantage is largest, because that advantage, compounded across a portfolio, is the return.
